EXTRA CLASS · COLORS

Every color, with its lesson on the card.

The color deck: eleven first colors walk in file order — red to gold, the colors a child names first — and then the deck grows up with four shades that are made, not found, each with its own mixing recipe. Every tile below opens its own simple lesson a kid can follow.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Every color — with a lesson on its card.

The Colors class is a bonus class, kept beside the main learning path like the Animal Categories and the Doctor Visit: the regular classes stay the core sequence, and this one is for the days when somebody asks what color is that? Fifteen spotter sheets — eleven first colors and four make-it-yourself shades — each one a two-by-two sheet of four labeled things in one color. Sixty labeled pictures in one deck: the red apple, the yellow sun, the grey elephant, the gold honey pot, and every square between. Each card opens a simple lesson a kid can follow: what the color is, where it hides in your house, and one way to hunt it tonight.

The deck runs in file order on purpose. It starts with red — usually the first color word a child learns — and walks through blue, yellow, green, orange, purple, pink, brown, black, grey and gold, ending on the shiny treasure card. Then the deck grows up: four shades that are not found but made — light blue, navy, peach and lavender — each with its own mixing recipe, for bigger spotters.

THE FIRST COLORS, ELEVEN WALKS

Eleven color cards, file order one to eleven.

The eleven colors a child names first, in the deck’s own order — red to gold, one card per page. Tap any picture and it opens its own simple lesson: the original card on the left, the kid-followable guide on the right.

RedBlueYellowGreenOrangePurplePinkBrownBlackGreyGold
MORE COLORS (AGES 4-5)

More colors (ages 4-5).

Four shades for bigger spotters — and a bigger idea: these colors are not found, they are MADE. Light blue is blue plus white, navy is blue gone dark, peach is orange gone soft, lavender is purple gone pale. Every shade lesson teaches its recipe — and mixing them for real is the whole game.

Light BlueNavyPeachLavender
THE CLASS GAME

The Color Hunt: turn the house into the deck.

Pick one card — say, the red one — and hunt its color all day: clothes, cups, cars, cushions, the crust on toast. Every find is called out loud: red car! red cup! red sock! Count the finds as you go and try to beat yesterday’s total. Then swap cards tomorrow — gold days hunt crowns and door handles, grey days hunt elephants and pavement. The house reshuffles itself into a new color lesson every single morning — and the day’s winner picks dinner’s plate color, which is exactly as powerful as it sounds.

SAME COLOR, TWO NAMES

Grey and gray. Both are right.

Colors carry their names across oceans like passports, and this class says so out loud. The card says grey — the UK spelling — while families in the US write gray: same gentle elephant-cloud color, two spellings, both correct. The glossy purple vegetable is an eggplant in the US and an aubergine in the UK. Whichever your family says, your child hears both — and learns early that colors, like words, come in families.

SUPPORTING RESOURCE

Print the color cards.

Every lesson has a matching flashcard in the library: the original artwork as a printable card with a download button and short notes for grown-ups. Keep the deck in the play corner — all fifteen colors, sorted and ready.

Age ranges are a guide, not a test. The age pill on every card is an honest hint, not a rule: the eleven first colors ride Ages 2+ — they are pointing-and-naming cards, the first words a toddler learns — and the four shades ride Ages 4–5, because each one is a mixing recipe with two ingredients to hold in mind. Any card a child loves is the right card today.

THE ROOM THAT PAINTS WITH THESE COLORS

Step into the Art Room.

The Colors class hunts every shade the house hides — and the school’s Art Room is where those colors become things: twenty-seven supply cards from crayons to watercolors, each with its own make-it activity. Mix two colors on the palette card, paint a bright background with the brush, dab clouds with cotton balls — every supply has a short page, a full lesson and a printable card, and the whole room rides on ages 2–5. Naming colors here, making with them there: the two shelves finish each other.

COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Red — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the color red: what it is, where it hides, and how to hunt it.

What is this?

Red is a color — the color of the apple, the fire truck, the ladybug and the strawberry on the card. Colors are words for how things LOOK, and red is usually the very first color word a child learns.

What does it mean?

Red is the color that shouts: stop signs are red, fire trucks are red, ripe strawberries are red. Your brain learned "red means look at me" long before you had a word for it.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "red", point at red things, and sort red from not-red. Four red things on the card is four repetitions of the same word — that is how the word sticks.

Why this matters

Color words are classification — the first science a child does. Naming red is sorting the world into groups, and sorting is the skill behind counting, reading and tidying up.

What it teaches

Vocabulary (one loud word, four anchors), visual discrimination (red versus not-red), and categorizing — the same muscle that sorts socks and letters later.

Words to learn

redapplefire truckladybugstrawberryhuntfindmatchspotsort

Say this to your child

“"Red! Say it loud — RED. The apple is red, the truck is red, the ladybug is red, the strawberry is red. Red is the color that says LOOK AT ME. Ready to hunt? First one to find something red gets a strawberry!"”

Step by step

  1. Hold the card up and point at each square, saying the word: apple — red, fire truck — red, ladybug — red, strawberry — red.
  2. Ask your child to point: "where is the red fire truck?" Then swap: they ask, you point (get one wrong on purpose — being the teacher is thrilling).
  3. The red hunt: walk the house and find five red things together. Count them out loud on the way.
  4. Snack the lesson: a strawberry or apple slice, named red before the first bite. Colors you eat stick deepest.
  5. Close by flipping the question: "what is NOT red on this card?" Trick question — everything is red! Laugh, then spot one not-red thing in the room.

Look closer at the picture

Look at the card closely: all four squares are different KINDS of red things — a fruit you eat, a truck that races, a bug that crawls, a berry you pick. One word covers them all. That is what color words can do.

Ask your child

"Which red thing on the card can fly?" (ladybug — well, flutter!) "Which red thing has a ladder?" (fire truck) "Which red thing do we eat?" (apple and strawberry)

What your child can say or do

Your child might start calling every round red thing "a strawberry" for a week, or point at the fire truck square and make the siren noise. Both are the lesson working.

Out in the real world

Fire trucks are red in the US, the UK and Canada — and the stop sign is red on three continents. The card’s reds are the ones your child will meet out the front door.

Try it together

Red light, green light, card edition: hold the red card up — everyone freezes. (The green lesson will bring the running. For now: freeze, giggle, freeze.)

Understanding check

Ask: "what color is the fire truck?" (red!) "Find something red in this room." (the hunt says it worked) "Is the sky red?" (no — silly, and sillies are learning)

This lesson pairs with the Red flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.

COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Blue — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the color blue: the color of the sky, the sea and the biggest animal alive.

What is this?

Blue is a color — the color of the whale, the umbrella, the balloon and the bluebird on the card. It is the color of the sky on a clear day and the deep sea where the real whales swim.

What does it mean?

Blue is the big-and-calm color: oceans, skies, the whale that is the largest animal that has ever lived. When your child says "blue", they are naming the biggest things they know.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "blue", find blue things high and low, and notice that blue lives on animals (whale, bluebird), things (umbrella, balloon) and the sky itself.

Why this matters

Blue is a favorite-color heavyweight in every preschool survey — a color a child LIKES is a color a child repeats. Repetition is the whole game at this age.

What it teaches

Vocabulary, sky-to-floor generalization (blue is not one object, it is a property many objects share), and a first joke about names: a bluebird is BIRD named BLUE.

Words to learn

bluewhaleumbrellaballoonbluebirdskysplashflybigfloat

Say this to your child

“"Blue! The whale is blue — the BIGGEST animal in the whole world. The umbrella is blue, the balloon is blue, the bluebird is blue. Blue is the color of the sky. What else can you find that is blue?"”

Step by step

  1. Point and name each square: whale — blue, umbrella — blue, balloon — blue, bluebird — blue. Add the sounds: whoosh, plop, whee, tweet.
  2. Look out the window together: "what color is the sky today?" If it is blue, the card just met the real world.
  3. Blue hunt: find three blue things in the room — one up high, one down low, one on your child (socks are famous for this).
  4. The name game: "the bird is blue AND it is called a bluebird! What would a red bird be called?" (A redbird! A cardinal IS one!)
  5. Close with the whale: the biggest animal ever, and it is blue — stretch arms wide as it will go.

Look closer at the picture

Three of the four squares FLY or float — the balloon floats, the bird flies, the whale swims, and the umbrella catches rain. Blue is the traveling color on this card.

Ask your child

"Which blue thing is the biggest animal in the world?" (whale) "Which blue thing do we open when it rains?" (umbrella) "What color is the sky?" (blue — usually!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might announce "BLUE SKY!" at the window for the next month, or insist the bath whale is the card whale’s cousin. Both are exactly right.

Out in the real world

Blue whales are really blue-ish grey — but "blue whale" is the name, and the card’s blue is the fair color for the biggest splash. Real bluebirds live across North America; UK families meet blue tits, the same idea in a smaller coat.

Try it together

Keep the balloon up: every tap must be announced — "BLUE!" — before the hand lands. Drop the balloon, say the word three times, back to the game.

Understanding check

Ask: "what color is the whale?" (blue) "Point at something blue in this room." (the hunt again) "Is a banana blue?" (no — and the giggle confirms the sorting works)

This lesson pairs with the Blue flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.

COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Yellow — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the color yellow: the sun’s color, the duck’s color, the smile in the crayon box.

What is this?

Yellow is a color — the color of the sun, the banana, the duck and the star on the card. It is the brightest color in the box, the one that looks like light.

What does it mean?

Yellow is the daytime color: the sun makes it, bananas ripen in it, stars shine it. When your child names yellow, they are naming bright and warm and awake.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "yellow", match yellow things to yellow things, and meet the two famous yellows UP (sun, star) and the two famous yellows DOWN (banana, duck).

Why this matters

Yellow is the easiest color to see — that is why warning signs wear it and why the school bus wears it in North America. Your child is learning the most visible word in the set.

What it teaches

Vocabulary, up/down pairing (sky squares and floor squares), and snack-time anchoring — colors attached to food memory last longest.

Words to learn

yellowsunbananaduckstarbrightshinequacksmilelight

Say this to your child

“"Yellow! The sun is yellow, the banana is yellow, the duck is yellow, the star is yellow. Yellow is the brightest color in the whole box. Quack like the yellow duck! Reach up like the yellow sun!"”

Step by step

  1. Point and name: sun — yellow, banana — yellow, duck — yellow, star — yellow. Quack at the duck. Everybody. No exceptions.
  2. Up and down: the sun and star live in the sky squares, the banana and duck live down here. Ask your child to point UP for sun, DOWN for duck.
  3. Snack the lesson: banana slices, and the word "yellow" said before every bite. Count the bites while you are at it.
  4. Star hunt: find the stars in your house — on books, pajamas, stickers. Stars are yellow even when they are drawn.
  5. Close with the sun stretch: reach tall like sunbeams, then curl small like a banana. Two shapes, one color.

Look closer at the picture

Every square on this card is SMILING — the sun has a face, the star has a face, even the banana looks pleased. Yellow is the happy color, and the artist knew it.

Ask your child

"Which yellow thing shines in the sky in the morning?" (sun) "Which yellow thing do we peel?" (banana) "Who says quack?" (duck — loudly)

What your child can say or do

Your child might start pointing at every egg yolk and banana with "YELLOW!" pride, or draw you a yellow sun for the fridge. Hang the sun. Always hang the sun.

Out in the real world

School buses are yellow in the US and Canada because yellow is the easiest color to SEE — the same reason the sun square is easy to spot first on the card.

Try it together

Duck, duck, YELLOW: the classic game with one tweak — the chaser says duck… duck… YELLOW, and the yellow call means chase. Same game, one color word drilled per lap.

Understanding check

Ask: "what color is the sun on the card?" (yellow) "Find something yellow at the table." (banana usually wins) "Does the duck say moo?" (NO — quack! and the correction is the learning)

This lesson pairs with the Yellow flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.

COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Green — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the color green: the color of leaves, frogs and lunchbox vegetables.

What is this?

Green is a color — the color of the leaf, the frog, the cucumber and the turtle on the card. It is the color of growing things: nearly every plant wears green while it grows.

What does it mean?

Green is the go-and-grow color: traffic lights say GO in green, gardens grow in green, frogs hop in green. Your child is learning the color of alive-and-happening.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "green", notice green outside (leaves, grass), and meet green on an animal (frog), a plant part (leaf), a vegetable (cucumber) and a reptile (turtle).

Why this matters

Green is the color children meet OUTSIDE more than inside — this card is the bridge from kitchen-table colors to park-walk colors.

What it teaches

Vocabulary, indoor-outdoor transfer (the card’s green matches the real grass), and movement anchoring — hopping while saying the word wires it deep.

Words to learn

greenleaffrogcucumberturtlehopgrowcrunchslowshell

Say this to your child

“"Green! The leaf is green, the frog is green, the cucumber is green, the turtle is green. Green is the color of growing things. Hop like a frog — fast! Now slow like a turtle… slooow…"”

Step by step

  1. Point and name: leaf — green, frog — green, cucumber — green, turtle — green. Hop once per square; the frog square earns three.
  2. The leaf question: "what does a leaf do before it turns brown?" It grows — green is the GROWING color. Any plant near the window is proof; go visit it.
  3. The crunch test: cucumber at snack time, word said first, crunch counted after. If cucumbers are outlawed in your house, any green vegetable drafts in.
  4. Speed game: frog hops FAST, turtle crawls SLOW — race both across the rug. The turtle always wins the slow race.
  5. Close at the window or garden: find the biggest green thing you can see together. Name it green, and name it yours.

Look closer at the picture

Two squares are animals in green suits (frog, turtle), two are plants and plant-food (leaf, cucumber). Green is the only color on the shelf worn by a whole kingdom — the plant one.

Ask your child

"Which green thing hops?" (frog) "Which green thing hides in its shell?" (turtle) "Which green thing do we crunch at snack time?" (cucumber)

What your child can say or do

Your child might croak at every green light, or announce the lawn is "a hundred leaves". Green pride is real — let it hop.

Out in the real world

Green means GO at crossings in the US, UK and Canada — a park-walk green light is this card waving hello. Frogs, turtles and cucumbers are green nearly everywhere on Earth.

Try it together

Frog hop path: cut five paper leaves, lay a trail, and hop leaf to leaf saying "green" per hop. The turtle finish (slow crawl to the couch) is the cool-down.

Understanding check

Ask: "what color is the frog?" (green) "What grows green outside?" (grass, leaves — whatever the window shows) "Is the turtle fast or slow?" (slow — with the matching crawl)

This lesson pairs with the Green flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.

COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Orange — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the color orange — a color with a trick: it shares its name with a fruit.

What is this?

Orange is a color — the color of the orange, the tiger, the carrot and the fox on the card. It is also a FRUIT — the only color on the shelf that is also a snack with the same name.

What does it mean?

Orange is red and yellow sitting together: warm like red, bright like yellow. The tiger wears it to hide in tall grass; the carrot grows it underground; the fruit and the color share one name.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "orange", know the word names BOTH the color and the fruit, and spot orange on two animals (tiger, fox) and two foods (orange, carrot).

Why this matters

A color with a built-in snack is a color that gets practiced at lunch — orange has more daily reps than any other color word.

What it teaches

Vocabulary with a double meaning (color AND fruit), animal movement vocabulary (prowl, trot), and the stripe pattern — tigers are orange with black stripes, a pattern word waiting in the wings.

Words to learn

orangetigercarrotfoxstripesprowlcrunchyjuicyfruitsame name

Say this to your child

“"Orange! The orange is orange, the tiger is orange, the carrot is orange, the fox is orange. A color you can EAT. Prowl like the tiger — quiet quiet quiet — then CHOMP like the carrot!"”

Step by step

  1. Point and name: orange — orange, tiger — orange, carrot — orange, fox — orange. Yes, the orange is orange. That sentence is half the lesson and all of the fun.
  2. The name story: the FRUIT came first! The color is named after the fruit, like peach (wait for the shade cards). Long ago people just said "yellow-red".
  3. Stripes spotting: the tiger has stripes, the fox has a white tummy, the carrot has a green top — same color, three different outfits.
  4. Prowl practice: stalk the hallway like the tiger on all fours, then trot like the fox, then curl small like a carrot. Guess which one gets the giggles.
  5. Snack the lesson: orange segments or carrot sticks — the word said first, the crunch counted after.

Look closer at the picture

Look again: two squares are FOOD (fruit, vegetable), two are ANIMALS (big cat, clever dog-cousin). Orange is the color of dinner and the color of the dinner-chaser.

Ask your child

"Which orange thing has stripes?" (tiger) "Which orange thing grows underground?" (carrot) "Which orange thing do we peel?" (the orange — and the peeling is the game)

What your child can say or do

Your child might answer "orange" to every "what is your favorite color" survey for a month, or roar at the fruit bowl. The tiger square does that to people.

Out in the real world

Tigers are the biggest cats alive and the only big cats that like water — orange on land, swimming in the river. Carrots are orange nearly everywhere, though the first ones were purple (the shade cards say hello).

Try it together

Fox and carrots: one fox (parent) guards the carrot pile (orange blocks or actual carrots), the cubs creep closer on each "orange…" whisper and freeze on the roar. Stealth plus the loudest word in the deck.

Understanding check

Ask: "what color is the tiger?" (orange) "What do we call the fruit?" (orange — same word!) "Show me a prowl." (the hallway knows)

This lesson pairs with the Orange flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.

COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Purple — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the color purple: royal, fruity, and made from two colors your child already knows.

What is this?

Purple is a color — the color of the grapes, the eggplant, the butterfly and the plum on the card. It is red and blue mixed together: the two loudest colors making one fancy one.

What does it mean?

Purple is the mixing-story color: long ago it was the rarest, most precious color in the world — kings and queens wore it because making purple was hard. Your child can make it with two paints.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "purple", spot purple foods (grapes, eggplant, plum) and one purple insect (butterfly), and hear the recipe — red plus blue.

Why this matters

Purple is the bridge card between naming colors and MAKING colors — the idea that pays off in the shade section, where every color is a recipe.

What it teaches

Vocabulary, two-into-one reasoning (red + blue = purple), and food vocabulary — eggplant is the US name, aubergine the UK one, both worth saying.

Words to learn

purplegrapeseggplantauberginebutterflyplumroyalmixbunchwings

Say this to your child

“"Purple! The grapes are purple, the eggplant is purple, the butterfly is purple, the plum is purple. Purple is red and blue mixed — the fancy one. Kings and queens wore it because it used to be SO hard to make!"”

Step by step

  1. Point and name: grapes — purple, eggplant — purple, butterfly — purple, plum — purple. Four purple things, three of them snacks.
  2. The recipe tease: "purple is red AND blue mixed. What do YOU plus red plus blue make?" Save the real mixing for paint day — the prediction is the lesson today.
  3. Grape count: ten grapes in a bowl, counted one at a time, each one purple. Counting plus color in one bowl.
  4. Wings moment: flap arms slowly like the butterfly from square to imaginary flower. Grape flower. Plum flower. Your child will name them.
  5. Two names for one vegetable: in the US it is an eggplant, in the UK an aubergine — say both, pick a favorite, both are right.

Look closer at the picture

The butterfly square is the odd one out — three snacks and one insect. Ask why the butterfly might want to be purple: to visit purple flowers without being noticed. Camo, gently introduced.

Ask your child

"Which two colors make purple?" (red and blue) "Which purple thing comes in a bunch?" (grapes) "What is the eggplant called in the UK?" (aubergine — a big word, say it proud)

What your child can say or do

Your child might declare everything purple is "for kings and queens" and start wearing purple to dinner like a coronation. Royal behavior is acceptable at the table and encouraged near the grape bowl.

Out in the real world

Plums and grapes grow in yards and markets across the US, UK and Canada; the butterfly is out in any garden from spring to fall. Purple food is real food — the card is a grocery list.

Try it together

Grape statues: music on, flap like butterflies; music off, freeze into a bunch — arms linked, standing still, purple and proud. Freeze games plus the word per round.

Understanding check

Ask: "what two colors make purple?" (red and blue) "Name a purple food." (grapes, plum, eggplant — any counts) "Flap like the purple butterfly." (the wings say it worked)

This lesson pairs with the Purple flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.

COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Pink — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the color pink: red’s soft cousin, the color of cupcakes and one very leggy bird.

What is this?

Pink is a color — the color of the flamingo, the cupcake, the flower and the pig on the card. It is red plus white: red’s gentlest setting.

What does it mean?

Pink is the celebrate color: cupcakes, birthday flowers, the pink of a pig’s nose. When your child names pink, they are naming treats and garden visits.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "pink", meet pink on two animals (flamingo, pig), one plant (flower) and one treat (cupcake), and hear the recipe — red plus white.

Why this matters

Pink is proof that colors are families: pink IS red, softened. The card quietly teaches that the color world has both loud and quiet versions of the same idea.

What it teaches

Vocabulary, recipe thinking (red + white = pink), balance (the flamingo stand) and a real science hook — flamingos are pink because of what they EAT.

Words to learn

pinkflamingocupcakeflowerpigsoftstandone legheartsnuffle

Say this to your child

“"Pink! The flamingo is pink, the cupcake is pink, the flower is pink, the pig is pink. Stand on one leg like a flamingo — one… two… three! And here is the secret: flamingos are pink because of what they eat!"”

Step by step

  1. Point and name: flamingo — pink, cupcake — pink, flower — pink, pig — pink. Two animals, one bloom, one treat.
  2. The recipe: pink is red plus white — like red took a deep breath and calmed down. Mix it for real on paint day; predict it today.
  3. The flamingo stand: one leg, arms as wings, count to three. Fall over? Flamingos do too. Try again, prouder.
  4. The secret: flamingos are born GREY and turn pink from the shrimp they eat. Your child eats carrots; the flamingo eats shrimp. You are what you eat!
  5. Close with the pig: a good snuffle noise, then a gentle nose-tap on the card. Soft like a pig’s nose, pink like one too.

Look closer at the picture

The cupcake square has a heart on top — pink wearing pink. And the flower’s center is a paler pink than its petals: one flower, two shades, the shade section waving from two cards away.

Ask your child

"Which pink animal stands on one leg?" (flamingo) "What made the flamingo pink?" (the shrimp it eats!) "Which pink animal says oink?" (pig — with feeling)

What your child can say or do

Your child might hold one-legged stands at every opportunity — waiting rooms, checkout lines, dinner. The flamingo stand travels well; be ready to join.

Out in the real world

Flamingos live in big flocks in warm places around the world; zoo visits turn this card into a real meeting. Pigs are pink nearly everywhere farms are — and smart as dogs, which the pig square’s grown-ups rarely expect.

Try it together

Flamingo says: like Simon Says but every command is a card square — "flamingo says stand on one leg", "pig says snuffle", "cupcake says wiggle", "flower says bloom". Four commands, one color, full-body learning.

Understanding check

Ask: "what color is the cupcake?" (pink) "How do you make pink?" (red plus white) "Why are flamingos pink?" (they eat shrimp — the fact they will tell everyone)

This lesson pairs with the Pink flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.

COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Brown — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the color brown: teddy-bear brown, pretzel brown, the color of warm and cozy.

What is this?

Brown is a color — the color of the bear, the pretzel, the mushroom and the coffee cup on the card. It is the color nearly every mixing pot makes by accident: brown is what happens when colors get friendly.

What does it mean?

Brown is the earth color: soil, tree trunks, teddy fur, baked bread. It is the most common color in nature and the coziest one in the crayon box.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "brown", find brown in toys and snacks, and hear the big idea — mix ALL the colors and brown usually arrives.

Why this matters

Brown has a marketing problem among kids and the card fixes it: brown is not boring, brown is BEARS. The coziest card in the deck gets the coziest lesson.

What it teaches

Vocabulary, a first theory idea (all colors mixed = brown), texture words (fuzzy bear, twisty pretzel), and snack anchoring — the tastiest color card by a mile.

Words to learn

brownbearpretzelmushroomcoffee cupteddycozyhugtwistwarm

Say this to your child

“"Brown! The bear is brown, the pretzel is brown, the mushroom is brown, the coffee cup is brown. Brown is the cozy color — teddy color, warm bread color. Where is YOUR brown teddy?"”

Step by step

  1. Point and name: bear — brown, pretzel — brown, mushroom — brown, coffee cup — brown. Three snacks and one bear; the bear is technically also a snack, for hugs.
  2. Teddy audit: fetch every brown teddy in the house to the rug. Name each one brown as it arrives. The pile IS the lesson.
  3. The big mix idea: what do you get when you mix ALL the colors? Usually brown — the mud color, the tree-trunk color, the color the whole forest stands on.
  4. Pretzel geometry: pretzels are twisty — trace the twist on the card with one finger, then twist arms and bodies into pretzel shapes. A knot is fine. Knots are the point.
  5. Close with the coffee cup: whose cup at home looks like that one? (Somebody’s always does.) Grown-ups raise the real one — the card’s toast.

Look closer at the picture

The bear square is the only one with a face — the pretzel, mushroom and cup are all things grown-ups make. Brown is the color of things we bake, and one thing we hug.

Ask your child

"Which brown thing gives the best hugs?" (bear — obviously) "Which brown thing is twisty?" (pretzel) "What grows brown in the forest, with a cap?" (mushroom)

What your child can say or do

Your child might line up every brown toy for a "brown parade" or demand a pretzel with scientific urgency. Both outcomes are the lesson succeeding.

Out in the real world

Pretzels are baked brown in ovens everywhere; real mushrooms grow in forests and — the safety note — only grown-ups pick them. The teddy bear is named after a president, Theodore "Teddy" Roosevelt, which is the square’s grown-up fact.

Try it together

Teddy picnic: blanket down, brown toys invited, real or pretend pretzels served, and every arrival announced — "the brown bear is here!" Sorting, naming, hosting. Clean-up is the bear parade home.

Understanding check

Ask: "what color is the bear?" (brown) "What do you get if you mix ALL the colors?" (usually brown!) "Find something brown in this room." (the teddy audit says it worked)

This lesson pairs with the Brown flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.

COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Black — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the color black: penguin suits, piano keys, the boldest color in the box.

What is this?

Black is a color — the color of the penguin, the piano, the black cat and the tire on the card. It is the darkest color there is, and it makes every other color next to it shine.

What does it mean?

Black is the bold color: tuxedos, pianos, night sky. Your child is learning the color that artists use to draw the OUTLINE — the color of edges and shapes.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "black", meet black on two animals (penguin, cat), one instrument (piano) and one thing with wheels (tire), and notice black-and-white pairs.

Why this matters

Black-and-white noticing is a real milestone — newborns see it first, and this card (with its white-bellied penguin and white-keyed piano) is full of the pair.

What it teaches

Vocabulary, contrast awareness (black on white pops), animal movement vocabulary (waddle), and a first instrument meet — the piano keys are a keyboard waiting to be touched.

Words to learn

blackpenguinpianocattirewaddlekeysnightshinesuit

Say this to your child

“"Black! The penguin is black, the piano is black, the cat is black, the tire is black. Black is the boldest color. Waddle like a penguin! Tinkle like a piano! Now sneak… like the black cat."”

Step by step

  1. Point and name: penguin — black, piano — black, cat — black, tire — black. Two animals, one instrument, one wheel.
  2. The suit story: the penguin’s back is black and its tummy is white — swimming below, hunters looking UP see white sky; hunters above see black sea. The suit is a disguise. Mind blown, gently.
  3. The keys game: the piano has black keys AND white keys — count three black keys on the card with one finger, plink plink plink, voice as piano.
  4. Waddle race: feet together, arms at sides, waddle the hallway saying "black, black, black". Penguins never run; the race is won by the best waddle.
  5. Close with the cat: quiet, sneaky, soft steps — the black cat lap back. Cats nap; so does the lesson. Good night, black.

Look closer at the picture

Every square hides a white part — the penguin’s tummy, the piano’s keys, the cat’s (missing here, but the tire’s tread pattern shows the road). Black never travels alone; it brings its contrast.

Ask your child

"Which black animal cannot fly but swims like a torpedo?" (penguin) "Which black thing has keys but no doors?" (piano) "What rolls and goes vroom?" (tire)

What your child can say or do

Your child might waddle on every errand for a week or plink out songs on the kitchen counter. The piano square’s fans are easy to spot — they are the ones drumming.

Out in the real world

Penguins live south — the Antarctic and up to South Africa and New Zealand; zoos bring the waddle to town. Pianos have 88 keys, 36 of them black — the number comes later, the plinking starts now.

Try it together

Black-key song: draw a paper keyboard, five white keys and three black keys, and "play" it while humming — every black key press must be announced: "BLACK!" Composing and color naming in one sitting.

Understanding check

Ask: "what color is the piano?" (black) "Waddle like the penguin." (the waddle confirms) "What is the opposite of black? Try white!" (the pair, named)

This lesson pairs with the Black flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.

COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Grey — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the color grey: elephant grey, cloud grey, the calmest color in the deck.

What is this?

Grey is a color — the color of the elephant, the cloud, the rock and the koala on the card. It is black and white mixed: the color between night and snow.

What does it mean?

Grey is the quiet color: clouds before rain, elephants padding through the savanna, stones on the path. When your child names grey, they are naming calm and heavy and soft-at-the-same-time.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "grey", meet grey on two animals (elephant, koala), one sky thing (cloud) and one ground thing (rock), and hear BOTH spellings — grey and gray.

Why this matters

Grey is the only card in the deck with a spelling story: the US writes GRAY, the UK writes GREY. Same color, two spellings — meeting both now prevents the later "which is right?" wobble.

What it teaches

Vocabulary plus a spelling note most preschools skip, heavy-versus-light reasoning (heavy elephant, light cloud — same color), and slow-fast movement vocabulary.

Words to learn

greygrayelephantcloudrockkoalastompfloatheavygentle

Say this to your child

“"Grey! The elephant is grey, the cloud is grey, the rock is grey, the koala is grey. Grey is the calm color. Stomp like an elephant — slooow and heavy. Now float like a cloud… soft and light."”

Step by step

  1. Point and name: elephant — grey, cloud — grey, rock — grey, koala — grey. Two animals, one sky, one ground.
  2. Heavy and light: the elephant weighs as much as a car; the cloud weighs almost nothing (it is made of tiny water drops). Same color, opposite weights — grey does not pick sides.
  3. Spell it both ways: say "grey" while tracing a G in the air, then the US way — "gray" — same word, different clothes. Both are right; families pick their own.
  4. The stomp and the float: stomp slow and heavy like the elephant (five grey stomps), then float to the sofa like the cloud. Heavy, then light.
  5. Koala close: yawn like the sleepy koala, hug like one too — koalas hug trees for naps. Choose a chair-tree. Nap optional, yawn mandatory.

Look closer at the picture

The elephant is the biggest land animal alive, and the koala is the sleepiest — it naps up to twenty hours a day. Grey is home to both the giant and the napper.

Ask your child

"Which grey animal is the biggest on land?" (elephant) "Which grey thing floats in the sky?" (cloud) "Which spelling does OUR family use — grey or gray?" (both are right!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might stomp everywhere announcing "ELEPHANT COMING" or yawn theatrically like the koala at bedtime. The koala yawn is a gift at tuck-in time — use it.

Out in the real world

Real elephants are grey; real clouds are white-grey-rainbow depending on the day. Koalas live in Australia and are NOT bears — the koala square’s grown-up fact, delivered with respect.

Try it together

Cloud watch: lie on the rug, look at the ceiling or the sky, and call the shapes — "that one is an elephant cloud, that one is a turtle cloud." Grey spotting, imagination, zero mess.

Understanding check

Ask: "what color is the elephant?" (grey) "Can you say it the US way?" (gray!) "Show me a heavy stomp, then a floaty float." (the room says it worked)

This lesson pairs with the Grey flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.

COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Gold — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches gold, the deck’s grand finale: yellow’s shiny cousin, the color of prizes.

What is this?

Gold is a color — the color of the crown, the sunflower, the trophy and the honey pot on the card. It looks like yellow but SHINES: gold is yellow wearing its fanciest clothes.

What does it mean?

Gold is the treasure color: crowns, trophies, honey, the sun itself if you catch it at the right minute. Naming gold teaches the difference between a plain color and a SHINY one — sparkle is a property, and gold has it.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "gold", hold yellow and gold side by side and spot the shine, and meet gold on two prizes (crown, trophy), one flower (sunflower) and one treat (honey).

Why this matters

Gold is the finish-line color of the first eleven: the deck ends on treasure on purpose. And the yellow-versus-gold comparison is real color training — noticing SHINE is noticing material, not just color.

What it teaches

Vocabulary, a material distinction (shiny versus flat — metal versus paint), and celebration vocabulary: the deck’s last first-color deserves a tiny ceremony.

Words to learn

goldcrownsunflowertrophyhoney potshinetreasurewinprizesparkle

Say this to your child

“"Gold! The crown is gold, the sunflower is gold, the trophy is gold, the honey pot is gold. Gold is yellow’s shiny cousin — the treasure color! You learned ALL eleven colors. Take a bow — and a golden medal!"”

Step by step

  1. Point and name: crown — gold, sunflower — gold, trophy — gold, honey pot — gold. Two prizes, one flower, one treat — the deck’s fanciest squares.
  2. Yellow versus gold: hold the yellow card next to this one. Same family — but gold SHINES. Ask: "which one would a king wear?" Shine-spotting is the lesson.
  3. Treasure hunt: hide one gold-ish thing (a spoon is perfect) and hunt it like treasure. The finder wears a paper crown to lunch. Non-negotiable.
  4. The honey fact: honey never goes bad — pots of honey found in old tombs are still good to eat. The honey pot square is holding a miracle.
  5. Close with the ceremony: every color learned today earns a golden imaginary medal. Count them: red, blue, yellow, green, orange, purple, pink, brown, black, grey, GOLD. Eleven medals. What a deck.

Look closer at the picture

Look for the shine: the crown has a jewel, the trophy has a star, the honey pot has a drip caught mid-pour. The artist made three squares GLISTEN — that is what gold does.

Ask your child

"Which gold thing do winners get?" (trophy) "Which gold thing do bees make?" (honey — the bees make it, the pot holds it) "Which looks shinier, yellow or gold?" (gold — and WHY: it shines)

What your child can say or do

Your child might wear the paper crown for days and award imaginary trophies to the toaster. Ceremony-first parenting: accept the toaster ceremony with full gravity.

Out in the real world

Real gold comes from the ground and never rusts — crowns from a thousand years ago still shine in museums. Sunflowers are gold and grow taller than most grown-ups; honey is the only food that never spoils. The card is three miracles and a flower.

Try it together

Golden treasure hunt (the repeatable version): hide three "golden" objects, draw a map with a big gold X, and hunt. The map is as fun as the hunt, and the X marks where gold lives — which is also square one of map-reading.

Understanding check

Ask: "what color is the crown?" (gold) "How is gold different from yellow?" (it shines) "How many colors did we learn?" (eleven — with the medal count)

This lesson pairs with the Gold flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.

COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Light Blue — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches light blue — the first SHADE on the shelf: a color you can MAKE.

What is this?

Light blue is a shade of blue — the color of the kite, the raindrop, the helmet and the cloud on the card. It is blue plus white stirred together: the sky on a soft day, the deep blue gone pale.

What does it mean?

Here is the big idea of the shade section: light blue is not FOUND in the crayon flap alone — it is MADE. Blue paint plus white paint, stirred slow, becomes light blue every single time. A shade is a color with a recipe.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "light blue", name the recipe (blue + white), and spot light blue high in the world — sky, rain, clouds, things that fly.

Why this matters

This is the thinking step up from naming: at four and five, a child can hold TWO colors in mind and predict the mix. Predicting is what scientists do — the shade cards are the first lab.

What it teaches

Prediction (what will blue plus white make?), following a recipe in order, and sky-words: light blue connects color to weather talk — rain, clouds, kites.

Words to learn

light blueshademixrecipekiteraindrophelmetcloudpalesky

Say this to your child

“"Light blue! It is blue plus white — the sky on a soft day. The kite is light blue, the raindrop is light blue, the helmet is light blue, the cloud is light blue. Shall we MAKE some? Blue, plus white… stir… LIGHT BLUE!"”

Step by step

  1. Hold the BLUE card and this one side by side. Two blues! Ask: "what is different?" (one is darker, one is lighter — pale, soft, washed-out).
  2. Reveal the recipe: light blue is blue PLUS WHITE. Say it like a magic spell — "blue, plus white… LIGHT BLUE!"
  3. Square hunt: the kite flies, the raindrop falls, the helmet protects, the cloud floats — four light blues that all live UP or come DOWN from up. Sky family.
  4. Mix it for real: blue paint, white paint, one spoon, one pot — stir slow and watch light blue arrive. Predict first, stir second, shout third.
  5. Close with the helmet question: why do kites and helmets share a color? (Both go fast and need to be seen!) Light blue is the look-at-me-in-the-sky color.

Look closer at the picture

The raindrop and the cloud are the same color but different SHAPES — one drops, one floats. And the kite has a bow on its tail. Light blue is the card with weather on it.

Ask your child

"What two colors make light blue?" (blue and white) "Which light blue thing falls from the sky?" (raindrop) "Which one do we wear to be safe?" (helmet)

What your child can say or do

Your child might mix a whole pot of light blue and paint the sky, the table and both hands. Hands wash; the recipe sticks forever.

Out in the real world

Bike helmets come in every color but light blue is a classic — and real raindrops really do look light blue against the window. The mixing recipe is the same one paint factories use, just bigger.

Try it together

Raindrop, raindrop, CLOUD: a duck-duck-goose variant — tap heads saying "raindrop, raindrop…" and the CLOUD call means chase, arms out, floating fast. Weather words ride along free.

Understanding check

Ask: "what is the recipe for light blue?" (blue plus white) "Point at something light blue in the room." (the hunt works for shades too) "Is light blue light or dark?" (light — and now they hear the pun)

This lesson pairs with the Light Blue flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.

COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Navy — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches navy — blue gone dark, the color named after the sailors who wore it.

What is this?

Navy is a very dark shade of blue — the color of the whale, the moon, the bow tie and the cap on the card. It is blue with a little black stirred in: the color of the sky when the last light leaves.

What does it mean?

Navy is the only color on the shelf named after PEOPLE AT WORK: the NAVY — sailors everywhere wear dark blue uniforms, so dark blue took the name. A color with a job history.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "navy", name the recipe (blue + a little black), and pair it with the light blue card — the two ends of the blue family, day and night.

Why this matters

Navy versus light blue is the deepest compare-and-contrast in the deck: SAME color family, OPPOSITE ends. Spotting "both are blue!" is classification — the real reading-readiness skill.

What it teaches

Comparing shades within one family, a word-history story (color names come from somewhere — navy from sailors), and night-and-day reasoning.

Words to learn

navysailoruniformwhalemoonbow tiecapdarknightdeep

Say this to your child

“"Navy! Blue gone dark — night blue. The whale is navy, the moon is navy, the bow tie is navy, the cap is navy. Navy is named after the NAVY — the sailors! Their uniforms were this blue, so the color took their name."”

Step by step

  1. Three blues in a row: light blue, blue, navy — the blue family from day to night. Point and name each; the middle card is the parent and the other two are its children.
  2. The recipe: navy is blue PLUS A LITTLE BLACK. Careful with the word "little" — one extra drop and you are in black. Recipes teach precision.
  3. The name story: sailors in the NAVY wear navy uniforms in every country’s fleet — the color took its name from the people. What would YOUR uniform color be called?
  4. Square talk: the whale dives deep where it is dark, the moon comes out when the sky turns navy, the bow tie and cap are the fancy navy clothes. Sea, sky, clothes — navy works nights and weddings.
  5. Close with the moon: find the moon out the window tonight if you can. If it is a crescent, say hello from the card.

Look closer at the picture

The whale on this card is navy, and the whale on the BLUE card is bright blue — same animal, two times of day. Ask which whale swims at night. That question IS the lesson.

Ask your child

"What two colors make navy?" (blue plus a little black) "What is navy named after?" (the navy — sailors!) "Which navy thing comes out at night?" (the moon)

What your child can say or do

Your child might rename the family pet "Captain" and demand a cap. Salutes are acceptable at dinner; the cap can be paper.

Out in the real world

Sailors’ navy uniforms are worn by navies worldwide — US, UK, Canada, everywhere ships sail. The bow tie is the navy’s fancy cousin for land celebrations. Real night skies go navy before black — watch for it tonight.

Try it together

Captain says: "Captain says anchor your feet… Captain says scrub the deck… Captain says navy night!" Navy commands, sailor obedience, one shade drilled per round. Bedtime version ends with "lights to navy — goodnight."

Understanding check

Ask: "what is the recipe for navy?" (blue plus a little black) "What is navy named after?" (the sailors — the navy) "Show me the blue family: light blue, blue, NAVY." (three hands, three shades)

This lesson pairs with the Navy flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.

COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Peach — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches peach — orange’s softest setting, and the second color named after a fruit.

What is this?

Peach is a soft shade — the color of the peach, the seashell, the kitten and the ballet slipper on the card. It is orange with white (and a whisper of pink) stirred in: the color of the fruit’s cheek.

What does it mean?

Peach is the SECOND fruit-named color on the shelf — orange borrowed its name from a fruit, and so did peach. Colors named after snacks are the tastiest words in the set.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "peach", name the recipe (orange + white, a touch of pink), and meet the deck’s softest card — three gentle things and one fruit that started it all.

Why this matters

Peach is where recipe-thinking gets delicate: not every mix is loud. Light blue was blue plus white; peach needs orange, white AND a pinch of pink — a three-ingredient recipe is a real step up.

What it teaches

Following a three-part recipe, texture and gentleness vocabulary (soft, fuzzy, gentle), and the fruit-to-color name chain — orange the fruit named the color, peach the fruit named the shade.

Words to learn

peachseashellkittenballet slippersoftfuzzygentlerecipetouchblush

Say this to your child

“"Peach! Orange plus white, with a hug of pink. The peach is peach, the seashell is peach, the kitten is peach, the ballet slipper is peach. Peach is the softest color — touch like you mean it, gentle gentle."”

Step by step

  1. Find the name-tag: the FRUIT in square one IS the color’s name — like orange! Ask: "which square is the color’s name-tag?" (the peach)
  2. The recipe: orange plus white, with a tiny touch of pink — say it in cooking voice, stirring an imaginary pot. Peach is a recipe you can almost taste.
  3. Softness tour: the shell is smooth, the kitten is soft, the slipper is ribbony, the peach is FUZZY. Touch-and-say: stroke your own arm gently — peach-gentle.
  4. The kitten game: tiptoe like a peach kitten, soft steps, soft voice — loud feet would wake it. The quietest minute of the whole deck.
  5. Ballet close: rise on tiptoe, arms in a ring, one slow twirl — a peach ballet slipper turn. Then a real peach for snack if the fruit bowl agrees.

Look closer at the picture

The peach in square one has a leaf — real peaches grow with leaves, and fuzzy skin. Everything on this card would be WARM to touch: shell in the sun, kitten, slipper, fruit.

Ask your child

"What is the recipe for peach?" (orange plus white, a touch of pink) "Which square is the color’s name-tag?" (the peach) "Show me kitten-soft tiptoes." (the quiet confirms)

What your child can say or do

Your child might pet every cat in the neighborhood "gently, like the card says" or twirl through the kitchen in sock-slippers. The ballet twirl has a long run-time; pace yourself.

Out in the real world

Real peaches are fuzzy to keep water off the skin — the fuzz is the fruit’s raincoat. Ballet slippers really are peach-pink so dancers’ feet blend like barefoot. And the seashell’s ridges all fan from one hinge — geometry on a beach.

Try it together

Peach-pass: pass a real (or drawn) peach around the circle — each holder says "peach" and one soft thing: "peach… kitten-soft", "peach… pillow-soft", "peach… puppy-soft". The word plus its gentle cousins, round and round.

Understanding check

Ask: "what is the recipe for peach?" (orange, white, a touch of pink) "What is peach named after?" (the fruit — like orange!) "Show me ballet-soft tiptoes." (the twirl says it worked)

This lesson pairs with the Peach flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.

COLORS LESSON · COLORS & SHADES · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Lavender — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches lavender — purple’s pale, powdery cousin, and the only color named after a flower.

What is this?

Lavender is a pale shade of purple — the color of the lavender sprig, the fairy, the teapot and the butterfly on the card. It is purple plus white stirred soft: the color of the garden at dusk.

What does it mean?

Lavender is named after the LAVENDER FLOWER — the only color on the shelf named after something you can GROW and SMELL. And purple was always the fancy color; lavender is fancy in slippers.

What does the child need to know?

The child needs to: say "lavender", name the recipe (purple + white), and meet the deck’s finale: a flower, a fairy, a teapot and a butterfly — the quietest squares in the set.

Why this matters

Lavender closes the shade section with the full arc: purple (red + blue) plus white makes lavender — a TWO-step recipe your child can trace backward. And the smell hook makes it unforgettable.

What it teaches

Two-step recipe reasoning (purple + white), sensory anchoring (a color with a scent), and a gentle-fantasy vocabulary — fairies and dusk gardens live here.

Words to learn

lavenderpurplepalefairyteapotbutterflysprigscentduskgentle

Say this to your child

“"Lavender! Purple plus white — pale purple, like the flower. The lavender is lavender, the fairy is lavender, the teapot is lavender, the butterfly is lavender. It is the only color you can SMELL. Sniff… ahh."”

Step by step

  1. Find the name-tag again: the flower in square one IS the color’s name — like orange and peach before it. The deck’s third fruit-and-flower named color.
  2. The recipe, two steps: purple is red plus blue; lavender is purple PLUS WHITE. Trace it backward: lavender came from purple, purple came from red and blue. Every color has a family tree.
  3. The smell: if a lavender plant or sachet lives nearby, smell it NOW — lavender is a color with a scent, which makes it the easiest shade to remember.
  4. Square flight: flap gently like the fairy, pour pretend tea from the teapot (pinkies up), flutter like the butterfly, and smell the sprig. Four squares, one sleepy garden.
  5. The grand close: line up ALL FOUR shade cards — light blue, navy, peach, lavender — and say the recipes together. Your child now knows colors that are MADE. That is the whole shade section, learned.

Look closer at the picture

The fairy holds a star wand and the teapot wears a flower — two squares with magic and manners. And the butterfly is back from the PURPLE card, one shade paler — same visitor, dusk edition.

Ask your child

"What is the recipe for lavender?" (purple plus white) "What is lavender named after?" (the flower) "Which color could you smell before you saw?" (lavender — the scent card)

What your child can say or do

Your child might sniff every flower asking "is this lavender?" for a month, or host nightly lavender tea parties for the fairies. Both are the deck’s finest graduation.

Out in the real world

Real lavender grows in gardens and windowsill pots worldwide; it scents drawers, soaps and calm bedtimes. Fairies live in every storybook that respects its readers. The teapot square pours imaginary chamomile — the traditional lavender-teapot pairing.

Try it together

Lavender tea party: set the toy teapot, invite the fairies (any small dolls or paper ones), and every pour needs the word — "more lavender tea?" The politest color practice ever brewed.

Understanding check

Ask: "what is the recipe for lavender?" (purple plus white) "Name all four shades." (light blue, navy, peach, lavender — with recipes if they are showing off) "What made the deck’s finale the best?" (it SMELLS)

This lesson pairs with the Lavender flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shades.
